ARISTOPHANES

CLOUDS

 

Translated by Ian Johnston

Vancouver Island  University

Nanaimo, British Columbia

Canada

First published 2008

Revised slightly and reformatted 2017, 2020.

This text is available as a PDF document at 
Clouds [PDF]
 and as a Rich Text Format document at 

Clouds [RTF]

Note that in the following translation the numbers 
without brackets refer to this text, while the numbers in square brackets refer 
to the Greek text. In the English text line numbers short indented lines are 
usually included with the short preceding line (as a single line) in the 
reckoning. Links to explanatory endnotes are indicated by an underlined 
number in brackets: e.g., 
(23)
. 
These have been provided by the translator. Stage directions have also been 
added by the translator.
 
In this translation, 
possessives of words ending in -s are usually indicated in the common way (that 
is, by adding 
-âs
 (e.g. 
Zeus
 and 
Zeusâs
). This 
convention adds a syllable to the spoken word (the sound 
-iz
). 
Sometimes, for metrical reasons, this English text indicates such possession in 
an alternate manner, with a simple apostrophe. This form of the possessive does 
not add an extra syllable to the spoken name (e.g., 
Socrates 
and 

Socratesâ
 are both three-syllable words; whereas, 
Socratesâs
 has 
four syllables).
 
 

The translator would like to acknowledge the valuable 
help provided by K. J. Doverâs commentary on the play (Oxford University Press, 
1968) and by Alan H. Sommersteinâs notes in his edition of 
Clouds
 (Aris & 
Phillips, 1982).

 

HISTORICAL NOTE

 

Clouds 
 
was first produced in the drama festival 
in Athensâthe City Dionysiaâin 423 BC, where it placed third in the competition. Subsequently, the 
play was revised, but the revisions were never completed. The text which 
survives is the revised version, which was apparently not performed in 
Aristophanesâs time but which circulated in manuscript form. This revised version 
does contain some anomalies which have not been fully sorted out (e.g., the 
treatment of Cleon, who died between the original text and the revisions). At 
the time of the first production, the Athenians had been at war with the 
Spartans, off and on, for a number of years.

 

DRAMATIS PERSONAE

 

STREPSIADES: a middle-aged Athenian

PHEIDIPPIDES: a young Athenian, son of Strepsiades

XANTHIAS: a slave serving Strepsiades

STUDENT: one of Socratesâs pupils in the Thinkery

SOCRATES: chief teacher in the Thinkery

CHORUS OF CLOUDS

THE BETTER ARGUMENT: an older man

THE WORSE ARGUMENT: a young man

PASIAS: one of Strepsiadesâs creditors

WITNESS: a friend of Pasias

AMYNIAS: one of Strepsiadesâs creditors

STUDENTS OF SOCRATES

[Scene: In the centre of the stage area is a house with a door to Socratesâs 
educational establishment, the Thinkery.
(1)
 
On one side of the stage is Strepsiades's house, in front of which are two beds. 
Outside the Thinkery there is a small clay statue of a round goblet, and outside 
Strepsiadesâs house there is a small clay statue of Hermes. It is just before 
dawn. Strepsiades and Pheidippides are lying asleep in the two beds. Strepsiades 
tosses and turns restlessly. Pheidippides lets a very loud fart in his sleep. 
Strepsiades sits up wide awake]

 

STREPSIADES

Damn! Lord Zeus, how this night drags on and on!

Itâs endless. Wonât daylight ever come?

I heard a cock crowing a while ago,

but my slaves kept snoring. In the old days,

they wouldnât have dared. Oh, damn and blast this warâ

so many problems. Now
 Iâm not allowed

to punish my own slaves.
(2)
 
And then thereâs himâ

this fine young man, who never once wakes up,

but farts the night away, all snug in bed,

wrapped up in five wool coverlets. Ah well,                                   

   10
   
  [10]

I guess I should snuggle down and snore away.

 

[Strepsiades lies down again and tries to sleep. 
Pheidippides farts again. Strepsiades finally gives up trying to sleep.]

 

STREPSIADES

I canât sleep. Iâm just too miserable,

what with being eaten up by all this debtâ

thanks to this son of mine, his expenses,

his racing stables. He keeps his hair long

and rides his horsesâheâs obsessed with 
 
itâ

his chariot and pair. He dreams of horses.
(3)

And Iâm dead when I see the month go byâ

with the moonâs cycle now at twenty
 days,

as interest payments keep on piling up.
(4)
                                      

 20

 

[Calling to a slave]

 

Hey, boy! Light the lamp. Bring me my accounts.

 

[Enter the slave Xanthias with light and tablets.]

 

Let me take these and check my creditors.

How many are there? And then the interestâ                                      

 [20]

Iâll have to work that out. Let me see now . . .

What do I owe? âTwelve minai to Pasias?â

Twelve minai to Pasias! Whatâs that for?

O yes, I knowâthatâs when I bought that horse,

the pedigree nag. What a fool I am!

Iâd sooner have a stone knock out my eye.
(5)

 

PHEIDIPPIDES 
 
[talking in his sleep]

Philon, thatâs unfair! Drive your chariot straight.                          

 30

 

STREPSIADES

That thereâs my problemâthatâs whatâs killing me.

Even fast asleep he dreams of horses!

 

PHEIDIPPIDES 
 
[in his sleep] 
 

In this war-chariot race how many times

do we drive round the track?

 

STREPSIADES

                                                
Youâre driving me,

your father, too far round the bend. Letâs see,

after Pasias, whatâs the next debt I owe?                                      
     

       [30]

âThree minai to Amynias.â For what?

A small chariot board and pair of wheels?

 

PHEIDIPPIDES 
 
[in his sleep] 
 

Let the horse have a roll. Then take him home.

 

STREPSIADES

You, my lad, have been rolling in my cash.                                    

   40

Now Iâve lost in court, and other creditors

are going to take out liens on all my stuff

to get their interest.

 

PHEIDIPPIDES 
 
[waking up]

                                             
Whatâs the matter, dad?

Youâve been grumbling and tossing around there

all night long.

 

STREPSIADES

                          
I keep getting bittenâ

some bum bailiff in the bedding.

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

                                        
Ease off, dad.

Let me get some sleep.

 

STREPSIADES

                                           
All right, keep sleeping.

Just bear in mind that one fine day these debts                                    

  [40]

will all be your concern.

 

[Pheidippides rolls over and goes back to sleep.]

 

                                              
Damn it, anyway.

I wish that matchmaker had died in painâ                                   

  50

the one who hooked me and your mother up.

Iâd had a lovely time up to that point,

a crude, uncomplicated, country life,

lying around just as I pleased, with honey bees,

and sheep and olives, too. Then I marriedâ

the niece of Megaclesâwho was the son

of Megacles. I was a country man,

and she came from the townâa 
 
real snob,

so
 extravagant, just like 
Coesyra.
(6)

When I married her and we both went to bed,                              

  60

I stunk of fresh wine, drying figs, sheepâs woolâ                                 

  [50]

an abundance of good things. As for her,

she smelled of perfume, saffron, long kisses,

greed, extravagance, lots and lots of sex.
(7)

Now, Iâm not saying she was a lazy bones.

She used to weave, but used up too much wool.

To make a point Iâd show this cloak to her

and say, âWoman, your weavingâs far too thick.â
(8)

 

[The lamp goes out.]

 

XANTHIAS

Weâve got no oil left in the lamp.

 

STREPSIADES

                                                                     Damn it!

Whyâd you light such a thirsty lamp? Come here.                          

 70

I need to thump you.

 

XANTHIAS

                              
Why should you hit me?

 

STREPSIADES

Because you stuck too thick a wick inside.

 

[The slave ignores Strepsiades and walks off into the 
house.]

 

After that, when this son was born to usâ                                           

 [60]

Iâm talking about me and my good wifeâ

we argued over what his name should be.

She was keen to add -hippos to his name,

like Xanthippos, Callipedes, or Chaerippos.
(9)

Me, I wanted the name Pheidonides,

his grandpa's name. Well, we fought about it,

and then, after a while, at last agreed.                                            

  80

And so we called the boy Pheidippides.

She used to cradle the young lad and say,

âWhen youâre grown up, youâll drive your chariot

to the Acropolis, like Megacles,

in a full-length robe . . .â Iâd say, âNoâ                                       
          

 [70]

youâll drive your goat herd back from Phelleus,

like your father, dressed in leather hides . . .â

He never listened to a thing I said.

And now heâs making my finances sickâ

a racing fever. But Iâve spent all night                                             

 90

thinking of a way to deal with this whole mess,

and Iâve found one route, something really goodâ

it could work wonders. If I could succeed,

if I could convince him, Iâd be all right.

Well, first Iâd better wake him up. But how?

What would be the gentlest way to do it?

 

[Strepsiades leans over and gently nudges 
Pheidippides.]

 

Pheidippides . . . my little Pheidippides . . .

 

PHEIDIPPIDES 
 
[very sleepily] 
 

What is it, father?                                                                                  

   [80]

 

STREPSIADES

                                               
Give me a kissâ

then give me your right hand.

 

[Pheidippides sits up, leans over, and does what his 
father has asked.]

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

                                  
All right. There.

Whatâs going on?

 

STREPSIADES

                              
Tell me thisâdo you love me?                          

  100

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

Yes, I do, by Poseidon, lord of horses.

 

STREPSIADES

Donât give me that lord of horses stuffâ

heâs the god whoâs causing all my troubles.

But now, my son, if you really love me,

with your whole heart, then follow what I say.

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

What do you want to tell me I should do?

 

STREPSIADES

Change your life style as quickly as you can,

then go and learn the stuff I recommend.

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

So tell meâwhat are you asking me?

 

STREPSIADES

Youâll do just what I say?

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

                                    
Yes, Iâll do itâ                                             

   110
   
  [90]

I swear by Dionysus.

 

STREPSIADES

                                                
All right then.

Look over thereâyou see that little door,

there on that little house?

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

                                                
Yes, I see it.

What are you really on about, father?

 

STREPSIADES

Thatâs the Thinkeryâfor clever minds.

In there live men who argue and persuade.

They say that heavenâs an oven damperâ

itâs all around usâweâre the charcoal.

If someone gives them cash, theyâll teach him

how to win an argument on any cause,                                          

  120

just or unjust.

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

                     
Who are these men?

 

STREPSIADES

                                                                       
Iâm not sure                      

  [100]

just what they call themselves, but theyâre good men,

fine, deep-thinking intellectual types.

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

Nonsense! Theyâre a worthless bunch. I know themâ

youâre talking about pale-faced charlatans,

who havenât any shoes, like 
 
those rascals

Socrates and Chaerephon.
(10)

 

STREPSIADES

                                       
Shush, be quiet.

Donât prattle on such childish rubbish.

If you care about your fatherâs daily food,

give up racing horses and, for my sake,                                          

  130

join their company.

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

                             
By Dionysus, no!

Not even if you give me as a 
 
gift

pheasants raised by Leogoras.
(11)

 

STREPSIADES

                                                      
Come on, sonâ                                 

 [110]

youâre the dearest person in the world to me.

Iâm begging you. Go there and learn something.

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

What is it you want me to learn?

 

STREPSIADES

                                                                  
They say

that those men have two kinds of argumentsâ

the Better, whatever that may mean,

and the Worse. Now, of these two arguments,

the Worse can make an unjust case and win.                                 

 140

So if, for me, youâll learn to speak like this,

to make an unjust argument, well then,

all those debts I now owe because of you

I wouldnât have to payâno
 need to give

an obolâs worth to anyone.
(12)

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

                                                              
No way.

I canât do that. With no colour in my cheeks

I wouldnât dare to face those rich young Knights.
(13)
                            

  [120]

 

STREPSIADES

Then, by Demeter, you wonât be eating

any of my foodânot you, not your yoke horse,

nor your branded thoroughbred. To
 hell with youâ                     

  150

Iâll toss you right out of this house.
(14)

 

PHEIDIPPIDES

                                               
All rightâ

but Uncle Megacles wonât let me live

without my horses. Iâm going in the house.

I donât really care what you're going to do.

 

[Pheidippides stands up and goes inside the house. Strepsiades gets out of bed.]

 

STREPSIADES

Well, Iâll not take this set back lying down.

Iâll pray to the gods and then go there myselfâ

Iâll get myself taught in that Thinkery.

Still, Iâm old and slowâmy memoryâs shot.

How can I learn hair-splitting arguments,                                  

                    [130]

all that fancy stuff? But I have to go.                                               

160

Why do I keep hanging back like this?

I should be knocking on the door.

 

 
[Strepsiades marches up to the door of the Thinkery 
and knocks.]

 

Hey, boy . . . little boy.

 

STUDENT 
 
[from inside]
 

                                      
Go to Hell!

 

[The door opens and the student appears.]

 

Whoâs been knocking on the door?

 

STREPSIADES

Iâm Strepsiades, the son of Pheidon,

from Cicynna.

 

STUDENT

                                
By god, what a stupid man,

to kick the door so hard. You just donât think.

You made a newly found idea miscarry!

 

STREPSIADES

Iâm sorry. But I live in the country,

far away from here. Tell me whatâs happened.

Whatâs miscarried?

 

STUDENT

                             
Itâs not right to mention it,                                 

 170
  
   [140]

except to students.

 

STREPSIADES

                                 
You neednât be concernedâ

you can tell me. Iâve come here as a student,

to study at the Thinkery.

 

STUDENT

                                         
Iâll tell you, then.

But you have to think of these as secrets,

our holy mysteries. A while ago,

a flea bit Chaerephon right on the eye brow,

and then jumped onto Socratesâs head.

So Socrates then questioned Chaerephon

about how many lengths of its own feet

a flea could jump.

 

STREPSIADES

                               
Howâd he measure that?                                   

  180

 

STUDENT

Most ingeniously. He melted down some wax,

then took the flea and dipped two feet in it.                                         

  [150]

Once that cooled, the flea had Persian slippers.

He took those off and measured out the space.

 

STREPSIADES

By Lord Zeus, what intellectual brilliance!

 

STUDENT

Would you like to hear more of Socrates,

another one of his ideas? What do you say?

 

STREPSIADES

Which one? Tell me . . .

 

[The student pretends to be reluctant.]

 

                            
Iâm begging you!

 

STUDENT

                                                              
All right.

Chaerephon of Sphettus once asked Socrates

whether, in his opinion, a gnat buzzed                                           

 190

through its mouth or through its anal sphincter.

 

STREPSIADES

What did Socrates say about the gnat?

 

STUDENT

He said that the gnatâs intestinal tract                                                  

  [160]

was narrowâtherefore air passing through it,

because of the constriction, was pushed with force

towards the rear. So then that orifice,

being a hollow space beside a narrow tube,

transmits the noise caused by the force of air.

 

STREPSIADES

So a gnatâs arse hole is a giant trumpet!

O triply blessed man who could do this,                                        

  200

anatomize the anus of a gnat!

A man who knows a gnatâs guts inside out

would have no trouble winning law suits.

 

STUDENT

Just recently he lost a great ideaâ

a lizard stole it!

 

STREPSIADES

                  
Howâd that happen? Tell me.                                               

  [170]

 

STUDENT

He was studying movements of the moonâ

its trajectory and revolutions.

One night, as he was gazing up, open mouthed,

staring skyward, a lizard on the roof

relieved itself on him.

 

STREPSIADES

                          
A lizard crapped on Socrates!                                

 210

Thatâs good!

 

STUDENT

                      
Then, last night we had no dinner.

 

STREPSIADES

Well, well. What did Socrates come up with,

to get you all some food to eat?

 

STUDENT

He spread some ashes thinly on the table,

then seized a spit, went to the wrestling school,

picked up a queer, and robbed him of 
 
his cloak,

then sold the cloak to purchase dinner.
(15)

 

STREPSIADES

And we still admire Thales after that?
(16)
                                              

   [180]

Come on, now, open up the Thinkeryâ

let me see Socrates without delay.                                                  

  220

Iâm dying to learn. So open up the door.

 

[The doors of the Thinkery slide open to reveal 
Socratesâs students studying on a porch (not inside a room). They are in 
variously absurd positions and are all very thin and pale.]

 

By Hercules, who are all these creatures!

What country are they from?

 

STUDENT

                          
You look surprised.

What do they look like to you?

 

STREPSIADES

                                                       
Like prisonersâ

those Spartan ones from Pylos.
(17)
 
But tell meâ

Why do these ones keep staring at the earth?

 

STUDENT

Theyâre searching out what lies beneath the ground.

 

STREPSIADES

Ah, theyâre looking for some bulbs. Well now,

you donât need to worry any longer,

not about that. I know where bulbs are found,                             

   230
  
  [190]

lovely big ones, too. What about them?

What are they doing like that, all doubled up?

 

STUDENT

Theyâre sounding out the depths of Tartarus.

 

STREPSIADES

Why are their arse holes gazing up to heaven?

 

STUDENT

Directed studies in astronomy.

 

[The Student addresses the other students in the 
room.]

 

Go inside. We donât want Socrates

to find you all in here.

 

STREPSIADES

                                            
Not yet, not yet.

Let them stay like this, so I can tell them

what my little problem is.

 

STUDENT

                                          
Itâs not allowed.

They canât spend too much time outside,                                      

  240

not in the open air.

 

[The students get up from their studying positions 
and disappear into the interior of the Thinkery. Strepsiades starts inspecting 
the equipment on the walls and on the tables.]

STREPSIADES

                                          My goodness,

what is this thing? Explain it to me.                                                      

   [200]

 

 STUDENT

That thereâs astronomy.

 

STREPSIADES

                                      
And whatâs this?

 

STUDENT

Thatâs geometry.

 

STREPSIADES

                                  
What use is that?

 

STUDENT

Itâs used to measure land.

 

STREPSIADES

                                
You mean those lands

handed out by lottery.
(18)

 

STUDENT

                                       
Not just thatâ

itâs for land in general.

 

STREPSIADES

                                   
A fine ideaâ

useful . . . democratic, too.

 

STUDENT

                                       
Look over hereâ

hereâs a map of the entire world. See?

Right there, thatâs Athens.

 

STREPSIADES

                                           
What do you mean?                              

  250

I donât believe you. There are no jury menâ

I donât see them sitting on their benches.

 

STUDENT

No, noâthis space is really Attica.
(19)

 

STREPSIADES

Where are the citizens of
 Cicynna,                                                        

    [210]

the people in my deme?
(20)

 

STUDENT

                            
Theyâre right here.

This is Euboea, as you can see,

beside us, really stretched a long way out.

 

STREPSIADES

I knowâwe pulled it apart, with Pericles.
(21)

Whereabouts is Sparta?

 

STUDENT

                                               
Where is it? Here.

 

STREPSIADES

Itâs close to us. You must rethink the placeâ                                

  260

shift itâput it far away from us.

 

STUDENT

                                               
Canât do that.

 

STREPSIADES 
 
[threatening] 
 

Do it, by god, or Iâll make you cry!

 

[Strepsiades notices Socrates descending from above 
in a basket suspended from a rope.]

 

Hey, whoâs the man in the basketâup there?

 

STUDENT

The man himself.

 

STREPSIADES

                           
Whoâs that?

 

STUDENT

                                                      
Socrates.

 

STREPSIADES

Socrates! Hey, call out to him for meâ                                                 

  [220]

make it loud.

 

STUDENT

                              
Youâll have to call to him yourself.

Iâm too busy now.

 

[The Student exits into the interior of the house.]

 

STREPSIADES

                                                       
O Socrates . . .

my dear little Socrates . . . hello . . .

 

SOCRATES

Why call on me, you creature of a day?

 

STREPSIADES

Well, first of all, tell me what youâre doing                                    

 270

 

SOCRATES

I tread the air, as I contemplate the sun.

 

STREPSIADES

Youâre looking down upon the gods up there,

in that basket? Why not do it from the ground,

if thatâs what youâre doing?

 

SOCRATES

                                               
Impossible!

Iâd never come up with a single thing

about celestial phenomena,

if I did not suspend my mind up high,

to mix my subtle thoughts with whatâs like themâ                             

  [230]

the air. If I turned my mind to lofty things,

but stayed there on the ground, Iâd never make                             

 280

the least discovery. For the earth, you see,

draws moist thoughts down by force into itselfâ

the same process takes place with water cress.

 

STREPSIADES

What are you talking about? Does the mind

draw moisture into water cress? Come down,

my dear little Socrates, down here to me,

so you can teach me what Iâve come to learn.

 

[Socratesâ basket slowly descends.]

 

SOCRATES

Why have you come?

 

STREPSIADES

                               
I want to learn to argue.

Iâm being pillagedâruined by interest                                                  

  [240]

and by creditors I canât pay off                                                        

 290

theyâre slapping liens on all my property.

 

SOCRATES

How come you got in such a pile of debt

without your knowledge?

 

STREPSIADES

                                              
Iâve been ravaged

by diseaseâIâm horse sick. Itâs draining me

in the most dreadful way. But please teach me

one of your two styles of arguing, the one

which never has to discharge any debt.

Whatever payment you want me to make,

I promise you Iâll payâby all the gods.

 

SOCRATES

What gods do you intend to swear by?                                           

 300

To start with, the gods hold no currency with us.

 

STREPSIADES

Then, what currency do you use to swear?

Is it iron coin, like in Byzantium?

 

SOCRATES

Do you want to know the truth of things divine,                                  

  [250]

the way they really are?

 

STREPSIADES

                                   
Yes, by god, I do,

if thatâs possible.

 

SOCRATES

                           
And to commune and talk

with our own deities the Clouds?

 

STREPSIADES

                                                   
Yes, I do.

 

SOCRATES

Then sit down on the sacred couch.

 

STREPSIADES
